new_flaws: pg_cron budget blown, and nobody owns it. design/data.md:60 justified ONE job ('miles_retention') by citing Supabase's <=8 concurrent jobs recommendation; calling.md:377 restates the same limit. Across the six revised siblings I count at least 14 distinct jobs: push-drain 10 s, the pure-SQL push_alerts alarm, push partition/retention drops (push.md:21/:77/:305); a DEDICATED 1 s call drain, the call_invites 1 h delete, call_signals + call_events partition drops (calling.md:24/:357); a 5 s push_pending drain plus net._http_response and cron.job_run_details prune jobs (messaging.md:179/:392); purge_expired hourly, a 5-minute user-delete cycle and a monthly orphan sweeper (crypto.md:80/:171/:244); couple_stream compaction and realtime.messages partition drop (transport.md:169/:254). Six domains each budgeted locally against a limit that is global. The domain that would have caught it is the unrevised one.

SIBLING-VS-SIBLING CONTRADICTION on the push queue, unarbitrated. revised/messaging.md Stage 9 (:179, :451) builds push_pending — keyed (couple_id, recipient_id), upserted with greatest(), a 5 s pg_cron drain, its own cached OAuth bearer table — and messaging.md:391 explicitly REJECTS the alternative: 'The original's per-message push_outbox did [grow with volume], and had no policy.' revised/push.md builds precisely a per-event push_outbox with dedupe_key and daily partitions, drained at 10 s. Both claim message-class push and both use the same collapse key m:<couple_id>. messaging.md's references to 'push.md' (L16, L508) are to research/push.md's Android platform facts, not to revised/push.md's design — the two were never reconciled. Schema ownership and migration ordering are the data/ops domain's job; it is unrevised, so this ships as whichever migration lands second.

FLAW 12's column-ACL landmine is being PROPAGATED by a revised sibling. crypto.md:244 (Stage 12) prescribes 'Server-set expires_at via table-grant removal plus column re-grant' — the identical apply-time-computed-column-list pattern verified at hardening_2026_08.sql:35-46, now extended to more tables. crypto.md:266 even quotes hardening_2026_08.sql:33 to justify it. It is the correct fix for clock trust and the correct trap for every future ADD COLUMN, and the CI assertion that would catch it (has_column_privilege over each table's non-protected columns) exists in crypto's verification for server-owned timestamp columns only, never as the general rule flaw 12 asked for.

The six revised designs consume a prerequisite that does not exist in revised form. 'supabase/migrations' and 'staging' appear zero times across revised/*.md, yet all six are structured as staged, revertible, independently shippable migrations. ROADMAP.md:120 makes Stage 0 (this domain) 'prerequisite for everything' and marks it ⚠ unrevised. Fatal 1 and serious 5 are therefore not merely open — they are load-bearing under six documents that assume they were closed.
verdict:
FAILS — there is no revised design to evaluate. E:/LDR/docs/architecture/revised/data.md does not exist; ROADMAP.md:9 and git e3432d1 both state data/ops was never revised because the session hit its usage limit. The only data plan on disk is the v1 the attack broke. all_fatals_closed is false by construction.

Scoring the four fatals against what actually landed: FATAL 2 and FATAL 3 are genuinely and well closed — by revised/push.md, a sibling. push.md:75 makes the outbox the retry owner behind a debounced immediate wake with the cron as a floor, raises call to ttl:45s, replaces profiles.fcm_token with push_devices, and states outright (push.md:182) that 'a message is never marked delivered because FCM accepted it', with delivery owned by push_receipts and UNREGISTERED classified terminal-per-device rather than dead-lettered. That is server-enforced, not client convention. FATAL 1 and FATAL 4 are fully open. Fatal 1 is untouched by anything: 'conformance', 'db diff' and 'relrowsecurity' return zero hits across all six revised files, so cron.job rows, retention_policy rows and storage.buckets.public are still unwatched, and crypto.md:218's one-time policy dump is a snapshot, not a recurring check. Fatal 4 is worse than untouched — the presence domain fixed presence, but design/data.md:169 still ships presence(couple_id, updated_at desc) in Stage 3 step 9, on a column revised/presence.md:98 deliberately does not have, on a table it retires.

That asymmetry is the real finding. Closure came from siblings acting locally, and only where a sibling happened to need it. Every flaw whose fix has no sibling owner is exactly as open as it was: the baseline/migration-repair ordering (5), the vacuous pg_policies assertions and the five tables with no DDL including app_secrets (6), client-writable retention timestamps (7) — where crypto.md:266 additionally rules the data design's proposed CI check defective and 'would have passed vacuously' — unindexed sweeps (8), the account-deletion cancel path (10, zero hits for account_deletions/cancel_my_deletion/data_subject_map anywhere), egress cost and the partitioning trigger (11), the profiles column-ACL trap (12, verified live at hardening_2026_08.sql:35-46), and the prod password in CI (14a). Flaw 9 splits: transport genuinely closed the broadcast half with realtime.messages RLS and private:true, and three separate siblings (messaging.md:518, push.md:408, presence.md:257) each independently declare the still-public couple_media bucket someone else's problem. It is this domain's, and this domain has no revision.

Consistency: the question does not quite apply, but the operative artifact — the v1, which is the only data plan anyone could ship — now contradicts revised presence (the index), revised push (a colliding push_outbox with the same name and different columns), and revised calling (a separate 1 h call_invites cron against the registry's 24 h single-job model). Two contradictions are between siblings and land here because schema ownership and cron budget are this domain's to arbitrate: messaging.md:391 explicitly rejects the per-event push_outbox that push.md builds, and the pg_cron count across six domains is ~14 against the <=8 both data.md:60 and calling.md:377 cite.

Big bang: Stage 0+1 remains the same big bang the attack named — repair marks production before staging has replayed anything, with auth and storage in scope — and it is now the undeclared foundation of six documents that never mention 'supabase/migrations' or 'staging' at all. Nothing here reconstructs a bug an earlier stage fixed, because no stage was rewritten.

Honest bottom line: two of four fatals closed by adjacent work, two open, eight of ten serious/minor open, four new cross-domain flaws created by revising around this domain rather than through it. Data/ops should be revised before any of the six ship, because it is the stage they all stand on.

still_open.flaw: F1 — messages.seq is one GLOBAL nextval sequence; no client migration step converts it, and step 4 persists a durable cursor over it.
still_open.why_still_open: No revised/client.md exists, so nothing in the client domain was changed. The server-side mechanism now exists THREE times over in siblings (transport couple_cursor.next_pos -> stream_pos; messaging chat_streams.last_seq -> messages.cseq; push couple_seq.last_seq -> cseq), all correctly allocated under a row lock. But nothing binds the client sync engine to any of them, the only client artifact on disk still cursors on `seq`, and the three counters are mutually unreconciled — so 'which integer is the client cursor' is now less determined than before the revisions, not more. Mechanism available next door; adoption unspecified. Not closed in this domain.

still_open.flaw: F2 — `messages` classified as an append-only log with cursor=seq; hide_message, delete_message_for_everyone (UPDATE) and clear_conversation_everyone (hard DELETE) mutate/remove rows without advancing it, and local SQLite keeps a cleared conversation forever.
still_open.why_still_open: Closed for the chat collection only, and only in siblings: messaging declares coverage over the ISSUED cseq interval and never derives it from rows, and makes clear consume a cseq; transport adds op='purge' and 'a stream position survives its entity'; push re-validates domain_row_id and marks rows superseded. The client design's generic collection taxonomy — the thing that classified messages as append-only and that drives the other ~14 registered collections — is untouched, and the taxonomy is the flaw. No sibling covers the non-chat collections (profiles, reasons, care, capsules, closer, cycle), which are owned by the also-unrevised data domain.

still_open.flaw: F3 — LWW cursor is (updated_at, id) with updated_at from Postgres now(), which is TRANSACTION-START time; an overlapping-commit reader advances the cursor past a row that has not yet committed and never sees it again.
still_open.why_still_open: Entirely unaddressed. Neither repair option (per-couple rev counter, or `updated_at > cursor - safety_window` with idempotent re-apply) was adopted anywhere. Transport asserts 'no clock enters any control decision' but only for its own `pos` stream and explicitly marks couple_stream.created_at display-only; presence removes its poll but says nothing about an LWW cursor rule. The client's LWW class — which step 7 applies to roughly ten collections — has no revised owner. This is the least-covered of the four fatals and remains exactly as the attacker described it.

still_open.flaw: F4 — Bootstrap does not terminate: 20-page cap -> 'too far behind' -> increment generation -> delete local rows -> restart at cursor 0, forever, for any couple above ~4,000 messages; and seq > 0 order by seq pages oldest-first.
still_open.why_still_open: The non-termination half is closed only along two specific sibling paths (transport's checkpointed resync: read head_pos=H first, page stream_pos <= H, set cursor := H; messaging's sync_bootstrap with a server-set install_floor above 2,000 behind). The client engine's generic 'page cap -> declare too-far-behind -> re-bootstrap' loop, which applies to every registered collection, is unrevised and is the actual loop. The oldest-first half is not fixed and is now contradicted: transport.md:245 pages 'ordered by stream_pos' — oldest-first — so a reinstalling partner still watches 6,000 messages replay before seeing the newest, which is precisely what the newest-first repair existed to prevent. Two siblings also specify two different bootstrap shapes for overlapping data.

still_open.flaw: F5 — Outbox created_at / next_attempt_at / expires_at are device wall clock; a phone whose RTC resets marks a just-typed message failed_permanent, contradicting invariant 12.
still_open.why_still_open: Genuinely closed by construction, but only for chat and only in messaging.md (#5): the outbox row has 'no timestamp column of any kind', persists `attempts` only, and schedules against a monotonic Stopwatch from process start, so there is no timestamp to corrupt. The client design's generic outbox — which routes reach, care, capsule, profile and every other mutation — is unrevised and still wall-clock. Partially closed; the pattern is proven and directly liftable.

still_open.flaw: F6 — Invariant 2 states `on conflict (id) do nothing returning *`, which returns ZERO rows on conflict, so an ambiguous-timeout retry cannot learn that the write landed.
still_open.why_still_open: Closed for chat in messaging.md: unique(couple_id, sender_id, client_msg_id) makes a retry a server-side no-op returning the ORIGINAL row, and the client treats 'any successful return including deduped: true' as landed. The client design's generic invariant 2, which every other collection's outbox path inherits, still says do-nothing. Partially closed.

still_open.flaw: F7 — Outbox queue_key is chat:<couple> with no hasMedia split; in a one-conversation app a stuck 30MB video blocks every subsequent text.
still_open.why_still_open: Not closed, and messaging's staging RECONSTRUCTS it. `queue_key` appears zero times in messaging.md. Stage 2 ships a text-only outbox with one main-isolate drainer; Stage 7 moves media onto the same outbox with no stated key split and no 'a stuck media op does not delay a subsequent text op' test case. Stage 2 is safe and Stage 7 re-introduces exactly the head-of-line blocking the attack identified — a later stage reconstructing a property an earlier stage held.

still_open.flaw: F8 — The doorbell is a request-amplification lever: a stranger who knows couple_id broadcasts doorbells and the victim's phone issues the resulting reads under its own JWT.
still_open.why_still_open: Half closed, and the closed half is the correctness half. Transport splits the doorbell onto server-write-only `cs:` with private:true and realtime.messages RLS, and its cursor rule makes a forged doorbell cost 'at most one redundant range query'. But transport then states the residue is 'a rate-limit problem, not a correctness problem, and the client single-flights and rate-caps its catch-up fetches' — that is client convention, which is not an invariant. Transport's actual token bucket is on the SEND path, sized in bytes/s against TENANT_MAX_BYTES_PER_SECOND; there is no server-side or by-construction cap on catch-up reads triggered by inbound doorbells, and the repair (doorbell may only set a dirty bit, never schedule work) was not adopted. Battery/quota amplification survives.

still_open.flaw: F9 — No data class exists for calls, games, heartbeat, touch, watch-together, proximity; invariants 5 and 13 read literally forbid them.
still_open.why_still_open: No third class is named in any document. Calling.md resolves the SDP question by making call_signals a durable server-ordered log (so invariant 5 is not actually violated for calls), but invariant 13 — 'no screen may issue a network request' — is now contradicted by two revised siblings: calling's in-call `call_keepalive` every 15 s and its gap-driven catch-up fetch are screen-driven, and presence's `presence_bootstrap()` fires on resume from the presence surface. Transport separately reserves an `rt:` bounded-lifetime high-rate topic for exactly this traffic without defining the class that governs it. The doctrine gap is still there, now with concrete violations sitting inside approved sibling designs.

still_open.flaw: F10 — Step 5 is a whole-codebase refactor (52 verified `.select(` sites across ~30 files, Result<T> at every repository boundary) presented as a 3-day lint and claimed parallelisable with steps 3, 4 and 7 that rewrite the same files.
still_open.why_still_open: Purely client-domain migration mechanics. Untouched — no revision exists. The ratchet repair (ship the lint as a warning with an allowlist seeded with every current offender, delete one entry per step-7 PR) was not adopted.

still_open.flaw: F11 — Steps 3, 4 and 7 are gated on a kill-switch that is an open decision, in a sideloaded app with no update channel; 'revertible' has no delivery mechanism behind it.
still_open.why_still_open: The mechanism now exists in presence.md Stage B — `app_runtime_config` (per-couple, presence_source, min_client_build), read over plain HTTP so it works with a dead socket, defaulting to legacy on read failure — and presence.md:542 states the residual honestly (a crash loop or a bug in the config-read path still needs a manual sideload). Transport.md:419 independently asks for a differently-named `app_config` row, so there are now two proposed config tables. No client-domain step is gated on either, and the distribution constraint is stated only inside presence, not in the client migration. Mechanism available; adoption unspecified.

still_open.flaw: F12 — Cost model contradicts open decision 4: 'under 2,000 messages/user/month' is arithmetically impossible while keeping Heartbeat (70-90 broadcasts/user/minute) and Watch-Together (24/min).
still_open.why_still_open: Unresolved. Presence re-prices its own domain (~6,200 billable/user/month) and messaging prices chat (7,200/user/month), but Heartbeat and Watch-Together belong to the unrevised data domain and appear in neither budget. The 9x reduction claim and the $25-30/mo saving at 1k users are still unsupported, and no committed client-side rate limit was moved out of open-decision territory.

still_open.flaw: F13 — IndexedStack keeps every tab mounted, so per-user always-on topics go from 5-8 to the union of all tabs; the missing invariant is 'exactly ONE realtime channel per device carrying only {collection, scope_id}'.
still_open.why_still_open: Not adopted, and now contradicted by the siblings rather than merely absent. Transport commits to four topics, three always-on (`cs:`, `cl:`, `dev:`, `rt:`) and argues channel count should be a function of the trust boundary, not one; presence adds `couple:<id>:live` and `couple:<id>:msg`; messaging adds per-recipient private topics; calling adds `call:<call_id>`. The one-channel invariant that would have made IndexedStack free is unavailable, so the <=100ms tab-switch claim still has no backing. Transport does close the related half by forbidding features from calling .channel() at all.

still_open.flaw: F14 — The layer-3 two-engine simulator is structurally incapable of finding F1, F2 or F3, because an in-memory fake server written the obvious way assigns seq in commit order and never hard-deletes under a cursor.
still_open.why_still_open: The repair was adopted in siblings but not here: transport names tests 3c (hard purge under the cursor) and 3d (bootstrap checkpoint against a concurrent writer), and messaging's property test #5 generates permutation, duplication, truncation and deletion of rows inside declared intervals. The client design's own verification section, and the requirement that the fake server be adversarial by construction with hostile behaviours enumerated as generator inputs, is unrevised.

new_flaws: ATTRIBUTION NOTE: no revised client design exists (revised/ contains only calling, crypto, messaging, presence, push, transport; ROADMAP.md:7-9 and :209 confirm the session ended before client and data were revised). Strictly, the revision introduced nothing because there is no revision. The items below are flaws that now exist UNOWNED — created by the six sibling revisions landing without the client design that was supposed to integrate them. They land squarely in the client domain.

FOUR unreconciled per-couple ordering primitives where the client engine needs one. transport: couple_cursor.next_pos -> stream_pos on entity tables + a couple_stream position log, catch-up via sync_head/head_pos. messaging: chat_streams.last_seq -> messages.cseq + an OPAQUE SERVER-MINTED COVERAGE TOKEN, with the explicit rule that the client merges the declared interval and 'has no code path that computes coverage from rows'. push: couple_seq.last_seq -> cseq on messages, reach_events, care_nudges, call_invites, consumed via fetch_since(cursor). calling: calls.signal_seq -> call_signals.seq. Cross-references are near zero: `cseq` appears 0 times in transport.md; `couple_stream`/`stream_pos` appear 0 times in messaging.md and push.md; push.md references neither chat_streams nor couple_stream. Concretely, `messages` would carry BOTH stream_pos and cseq, with cseq allocated from two differently-named counter tables in two different documents. The client's 'one generic sync engine, one cursor per collection' thesis cannot be built from these as written, and the cursor TYPE is inconsistent — an integer in transport and push, an opaque token in messaging.

Direct contradiction between transport and calling over call signalling. transport.md:71 states call signalling MOVES INTO THE STREAM (stream='call', entity call_signals) so ICE 'inherits commit order' and 'Glare resolves on pos — a total order both peers already have, server-assigned'. calling.md:52/78/103 keeps call_signals on its own per-call counter (calls.signal_seq assigned by trigger T3) and resolves glare by comparing p_call_id against live.id as a 128-bit total order, explicitly not on a stream position. Two revised designs specify two different orderings and two different glare mechanisms for the same table. Only one can ship.

Two competing server-read runtime-config tables: presence.md Stage B creates `app_runtime_config` (per-couple; presence_source, min_client_build) and declares it the revert mechanism for every client stage; transport.md:419 separately asks for an `app_config` row as its remote kill switch.
